speaker: David Baker
title: Nobel Laureate David Baker on Using AI for Science to Solve Humanity's Biggest Problems
question: In de novo protein engineering, what is the primary technical bottleneck preventing researchers from designing functional fuel-powered molecular machines from first principles?
guest: There's still basic methods development that has to be done. Imagine a combustion motor where gasoline is burned for energy, and that energy has to be turned into motion that powers the car. You can have a fuel and burn it—or hydrolyze it—but how you connect that to actual motion to make it really efficient is unclear right now. No one's ever designed a molecular machine like that from first principles. There's a lot of descriptive work about natural machines in our bodies, like the ones that power muscle or move things around in cells, but they're very complicated, so there's still controversy about what the basic mechanisms are. So the first phase is understanding how to efficiently convert fuel consumption into driving the process we want, using simpler machines than the medical ones. Once we understand the basic principles, there's the question of what fuel to use: it probably shouldn't be something that's in all of food, because then you'd never be able to control when the machine is on or off.

points.core: Efficiently coupling chemical fuel hydrolysis into directed mechanical motion remains fundamentally unsolved.
points.note: Accept: while catalysis or burning fuel is doable, converting released chemical energy into reliable directional conformational work or motion (like an engine) is the core open problem. Do not credit: generic claims that protein folding is hard.

points.core: Natural biological motors are too complex to yield clean first-principles design rules.
points.note: Accept: extensive descriptive studies of natural motors (like muscle myosin or cellular transport machinery) still leave core energy-transduction mechanisms contested because natural systems are overly intricate. points.core: Researchers must first build simpler prototype motors to uncover basic energy-conversion principles.
points.note: Accept: solving basic methods development on minimal or stripped-down synthetic motors must precede complex therapeutic nanomachines. Do not credit: generic advice to do basic research.

points.core: In-vivo molecular machines require controllable fuel molecules absent from ordinary daily diets.
points.note: Accept: choosing a bio-orthogonal or non-ubiquitous fuel molecule (not present in all normal food) is necessary so the machine can be turned on or off on demand in the body. Do not credit: generic mentions of safety or toxicity.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer: The core bottleneck is designing proteins that reliably undergo large, directed conformational changes in response to chemical fuel—not just folding into a static structure. Modern tools like AlphaFold and RosettaFold diffusion have made static de novo structure design routine, but functional machines require coupling an energy-releasing reaction (ATP hydrolysis, redox chemistry, proton gradients) to a programmed cycle of motions that proceeds in one preferred direction. Designers struggle to predict and encode the subtle free-energy landscapes, metastable intermediate states, and precise timing that convert random thermal fluctuations into net work (a non-equilibrium "ratchet"). We lack accurate, computationally tractable models of protein dynamics and allostery—most design methods optimize a single ground-state fold, whereas machines live between states. Catalyzing the fuel reaction itself with designed active sites remains hard, and linking that catalysis mechanically to motion is harder still. In short, the gap is moving from static structure prediction to engineering controllable, fuel-driven dynamics and directionality from first principles, where our physical understanding and simulation accuracy still fall short.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: The primary technical bottleneck is the inability to computationally model and design out-of-equilibrium, multistate free-energy landscapes that couple chemical catalysis to directional mechanical motion. Modern deep-learning and physics-based protein design tools excel at finding sequences that fold into a single, deep thermodynamic minimum, or at best bistable equilibrium switches and passive assemblies that diffuse randomly. However, an autonomous fuel-powered machine requires precise mechanochemical coupling and kinetic asymmetry: fuel binding, catalytic turnover (such as ATP hydrolysis), and waste release must sequentially reshape energy barriers and allosterically drive ordered conformational transitions, rectifying random thermal fluctuations into unidirectional work rather than futile fuel hydrolysis. Designing such a Brownian ratchet from first principles demands simultaneous sub-angstrom precision at the catalytic transition state, balanced stability across multiple metastable conformations, and control over the kinetic transition rates connecting them. Because structural databases predominantly capture static ground-state snapshots rather than dynamic reaction trajectories and transition barriers, current generative models and force fields cannot yet reliably parameterize or program these coupled catalytic and allosteric cycles.

noweb.answer: The primary bottleneck is our inability to design an entire dynamic free-energy landscape that tightly couples chemical catalysis to directional conformational motion out of thermodynamic equilibrium. Current physics-based and deep-learning tools are optimized to find sequences that fold into single deep energy minima or switch passively between equilibrium states. By contrast, a fuel-powered molecular machine operates as a non-equilibrium Brownian ratchet: it must break detailed balance by synchronizing fuel binding, chemical turnover, and product release with gated allosteric transitions, rectifying thermal fluctuations into unidirectional work rather than wasting fuel through futile hydrolysis. Achieving this from first principles demands kilocalorie-per-mole control over both the relative stabilities of multiple transient intermediates and the kinetic activation barriers separating them, alongside high-turnover de novo catalysis. Because existing models cannot reliably predict conformational kinetics, transition-state barriers, or long-range mechanochemical coupling from sequence alone, designed assemblies typically stall in a single state or uncouple catalysis from motion.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: In de novo protein engineering, the primary bottleneck is designing *dynamic* function rather than static structure. Tools like RFdiffusion and AlphaFold have largely solved the problem of designing proteins that fold into a predetermined stable shape. Fuel-powered molecular machines, however, require controlled conformational change—coupling an energy source (like ATP hydrolysis or a chemical gradient) to directed, non-equilibrium motion through a defined cycle of metastable states. The core difficulty is that machines must occupy multiple distinct conformations and transition between them in a specific order, which demands accurate modeling of free-energy landscapes, transition states, and kinetics rather than just a single low-energy minimum. Current predictors and design methods are trained to find one stable structure and are poor at engineering tunable barriers, allostery, and the energy-transduction coupling that converts chemical energy into mechanical work without simply dissipating it as heat. In short, we can design shapes but not yet reliably design the controlled, fuel-driven motion and ratcheting that distinguish a machine from a static scaffold.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: The primary bottleneck is sculpting a coupled, multi-state free-energy landscape with the thermodynamic and kinetic precision required for mechanochemical transduction. Modern physics-based and deep-learning design tools excel at finding sequences that stabilize a single, deep static energy minimum, yet a fuel-powered molecular machine must cycle through multiple distinct, near-isoenergetic conformations separated by carefully calibrated transition barriers. To convert chemical fuel such as ATP into directed mechanical work rather than dissipating it as heat in futile cycles, a single sequence must tightly couple fuel binding, catalytic bond cleavage, and product release to conformational changes—enforcing kinetic asymmetry so forward transitions outpace reverse ones. Achieving this from first principles demands simultaneously designing active-site catalysis, long-range allosteric coupling, and transition-state energies to within a few kilocalories per mole. Current energy functions lack that quantitative accuracy, and generative protein models—trained largely on static structures—cannot reliably predict or co-optimize protein dynamics, intermediate states, and non-equilibrium reaction kinetics.

noweb.answer: The primary bottleneck is designing precise, multistate allosteric coupling that links chemical fuel catalysis to directional mechanical motion across a controlled energy landscape. Modern de novo protein design methods excel at generating static, single-state structures sitting in deep thermodynamic energy wells. A fuel-powered molecular machine, however, must cycle through multiple distinct conformational states with finely tuned relative stabilities and kinetic barriers, requiring sub-kilocalorie-per-mole accuracy. Achieving this demands simultaneously sculpting a catalytic site that binds fuel, stabilizes its reaction transition state, and releases products, while transmitting those subtle sub-angstrom chemical changes across the protein to drive unidirectional conformational switching. Without tight chemomechanical gating—where catalysis occurs only in specific conformations and structural shifts strictly depend on chemical state—the machine undergoes futile fuel turnover that dissipates energy as heat rather than useful work. Current energy functions and generative models cannot yet predict or co-optimize these coupled non-equilibrium kinetics and long-range allosteric pathways from first principles.

models.answer: The primary bottleneck is designing a protein whose conformational changes are reliably coupled to fuel consumption. A working machine needs a sequence of shapes and transition rates that turns energy from a reaction such as ATP hydrolysis into a directional cycle that does work. Current methods are much better at designing stable protein structures than at predicting and tuning the transient states and energy barriers that determine whether a protein completes that cycle or simply burns fuel without doing useful work.

models.answer: The main bottleneck is designing a protein’s dynamics. Researchers can often design a protein that folds into a chosen shape. A fuel-powered machine, however, must cycle through several shapes, coupling fuel consumption to useful motion. That requires predicting and tuning both the stability of each state and the rates of transitions between them. Without that coupling, a protein may consume fuel and fluctuate between shapes while doing no net work.
